Paul Robert Milgrom (born April 20, 1948) is an American economist and the Shirley and Leonard Ely Professor at Stanford University, holding the position since 1987. He is also a professor in the Stanford School of Engineering and a Senior Fellow at the Stanford Institute for Economic Research. An expert in game theory, especially auction theory and pricing strategies, he won the 2020 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Robert B. Wilson for advancements in auction theory and new auction formats.

Milgrom co-created the no-trade theorem with Nancy Stokey and co-founded several companies, including Auctionomics, which offers software and services for commercial auctions. He and his advisor Wilson developed the auction protocol used by the FCC for allocating cellular frequencies. Milgrom led the design of the 2016-2017 broadcast incentive auction. In 2024, Auctionomics won a technical Emmy Award for contributions to spectrum auction design.

I’m skeptical that home affordability metrics like mortgage-to-salary ratios actually capture the real struggle—because they often ignore regional cost-of-living spikes, hidden fees, and the fact that many “affordable” homes are in areas with no jobs, transit, or schools.  
What if rising property values in urban centers aren’t a sign of healthy demand but a symptom of speculative investing and zoning bottlenecks that artificially constrain supply?  
And let’s be honest—using household income brackets to measure affordability assumes people have stable, predictable earnings, which isn’t true for gig workers, part-timers, or those in volatile industries.  
How many “affordable” mortgages are really just adjustable-rate loans that’ll reset into unaffordability once rates climb again?  
Are we mistaking low initial payments for long-term stability—or are we setting families up for future displacement when the balloon pops?  
If urban property values keep outpacing wage growth, then no ratio can mask the fact that ownership is becoming a privilege, not a milestone.  
And what about renters who get priced out before even qualifying for a mortgage—do these metrics even account for them, or are they just measuring who’s barely hanging on?  
At some point, calling something “affordable” based on outdated formulas becomes less analysis and more wishful thinking.

Sizable majorities of adults  strongly or somewhat favor  requiring electronic voting  machines to print a paper  backup of the ballot   $(82\%)$  ,  making early, in-person voting  available to voters for at least  two weeks prior to Election  Day  $(78\%)$  , and requiring all  voters to show government  issued photo identification to  vote   $(76\%)$  .

content.text: PEW RESEARCH CENTER  Women   $(59\%)$   are more confident than men   $(48\%)$   in Biden’s ability to deal effectively with  China. Black   $(82\%)$   and Hispanic adults   $(70\%)$    also express more confidence than White adults   $(43\%)$  . Those with a college degree expect  Biden will be able to deal effectively with China  at a higher rate than those with less schooling  (  $60\%$   vs.  $50\%$  , respectively).

Compared with 2020, concern about various China-related issues generally increased more among  Republicans than among Democrats. For instance, while the share of Republicans who say the loss  of U.S. jobs to China poses a very serious problem increased by 14 percentage points, there was no  significant change among Democrats. On issues where concern rose overall, increases tended to be  especially steep among conservative Republicans.

Across age groups, older Americans express more concern about China-related issues. Americans  ages 65 and older are at least 20 points more likely than those ages 18 to 29 to say most issues  asked about in the survey are  very  serious problems.

content.text: About four-in-ten Americans see the U.S. trade deficit with China – which decreased for  the  second year in a row  – as a very serious problem, unchanged from 2020. conversation.content: Public opinion on international institutions like the EU, NATO, and Russia varies dramatically across nations—not just because of policy, but because of historical memory, economic stakes, and cultural alignment. In Western Europe, the EU is often seen as a stabilizing force, while in Eastern Europe, NATO carries more emotional weight as a shield against Russian influence. Meanwhile, countries like Hungary or Serbia show ambivalence, where nationalist narratives clash with institutional loyalty. Russia’s image shifts from “threat” in the Baltics to “strategic partner” in parts of Africa and Asia—reflecting how geopolitical alignment is less about ideology and more about perceived benefit. Even within democracies, trust in these institutions isn’t monolithic: younger generations may view NATO as outdated, while older voters see it as essential. What’s clear is that public sentiment isn’t static—it’s shaped by media, crisis response, and whether citizens feel these bodies serve their interests or distant elites. The real divide isn’t just East vs. West—it’s between those who believe in multilateralism as a tool for security and those who see it as a constraint on sovereignty.
conversation.subtopic: Cross-national public opinion differences on international institutions, especially the EU, NATO, and Russia.

conversation.content: It’s fascinating how public opinion on institutions like the EU and NATO isn’t just about policy—it’s deeply tied to lived experience, historical trauma, and economic self-interest. In Poland or the Baltics, NATO isn’t an abstract alliance; it’s a psychological safety net shaped by decades of Soviet-era fear. Meanwhile, in France or Germany, the EU is often framed as bureaucratic overreach—until a crisis hits and its coordination power suddenly feels indispensable. Russia’s global image is even more fluid: condemned in Kyiv, courted in Cairo, and quietly respected in parts of Latin America where Western sanctions feel like hypocrisy. What’s often overlooked is how younger voters across Europe are less invested in institutional loyalty and more focused on whether these bodies deliver tangible benefits—like climate action or digital rights—rather than symbolic unity. The real tension isn’t East vs. West—it’s between those who see multilateralism as a shield and those who view it as a straitjacket. And if institutions don’t adapt to that generational shift, they risk becoming relics admired by diplomats but ignored by citizens.

Whether frontline employees notice a shift in how decisions are made, not just who’s signing the memos.

And let’s be real: if employees still feel like their feedback gets ignored or their safety concerns get buried under quarterly targets, no amount of “governance updates” will mean squat. Real change would show up in daily operations—not press releases. Until power shifts from the corner office to the people actually doing the work, these moves are just corporate theater. The true test isn’t who’s signing the memos—it’s whether the person filling out the TPS report feels heard, safe, and valued. If governance doesn’t alter who controls decisions or how accountability flows, then it’s not reform—it’s rebranding dysfunction. And honestly, if we keep pretending title changes equal transformation, we’re not solving problems—we’re just staging them better.
conversation.subtopic: Corporate leadership transitions and executive role assignments as part of organizational governance updates.

conversation.content: Take Wells Fargo: firing the CEO didn’t stop fake accounts until they killed the sales quotas that drove fraud. Uber’s 2017 overhaul worked because bonuses were tied to culture metrics like retention—not just stock price. Boeing’s leadership swaps failed until regulators forced engineering back into decision-making, proving real change needs structural redesign, not just new titles. If frontline workers still feel ignored or pressured to cut corners, no governance update matters—power has to shift, not just names.

This image is an infographic titled **"Home Affordability"** with a focus on the Chicago area, as indicated by the map in the center. The infographic is divided into several sections, each presenting different data visualizations related to home affordability.

### Main Sections and Details:

#### 1. **Map (Center)**

- The shading represents different levels of home affordability, with a legend indicating "Very High," "High," "Average," "Low," and "Very Low" affordability.
- The map is branded with the "esri" logo in the bottom right corner.

#### 2. **Workforce Profile (Left)**
- A horizontal bar chart displays the percentage of the workforce in various sectors for Cook County.
- Sectors listed (top to bottom): Agriculture, Mining, Construction, Manufacturing, Wholesale Trade, Retail Trade, Transportation, Utilities, Information, Finance/Insurance, Real Estate, Professional/Tech Services, Management, Admin/Waste Mgmt, Educational Services, Health Care, Arts/Entertainment/Rec, Accommodation/Food Services, Public Administration, Other Services.

#### 3. **Pie Charts (Bottom)**
- **Educational Attainment:** Pie chart with segments for No High School, High School Graduate, Some College, Associate Degree, Bachelor’s Degree, Graduate/Prof.

- **Household Income:** Bar chart with x-axis labeled in income ranges ($15,000, $35,000, $55,000, $75,000, $100,000, $150,000, $200,000+), with the highest bars at $55,000 and $75,000.

#### 5. **General Layout and Design**
- The background is a dark shade, with white and light gray text and chart elements.

- The source is cited at the bottom right: "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Census 2010 Summary File 1; Esri forecasts for 2017 and 2022."

- The infographic is visually balanced, with the map as the central focus, surrounded by supporting data visualizations.

- The data is specific to Cook County, as noted in the Workforce Profile section.

conversation.content: Public perception gaps between nations on global institutions often stem from how those institutions are experienced locally—whether they’re seen as enforcers of fairness or tools of Western dominance. In places like Nigeria or Indonesia, the IMF’s austerity demands can feel like economic colonization, while in Germany or Canada, similar policies might be framed as necessary discipline. These divergent views aren’t just about policy—they’re rooted in historical power imbalances, cultural narratives, and whether local populations feel consulted or coerced. What’s fascinating is how social media amplifies these divides: a protest in Lagos against World Bank loan conditions gets framed as anti-globalization in Western headlines, while in Jakarta, it’s seen as reclaiming sovereignty. The legitimacy crisis isn’t about incompetence—it’s about who gets to define “success” and whose pain is deemed acceptable collateral. Realignment won’t come from PR overhauls or leadership swaps at the UN or WTO; it requires redistributing decision-making power so that voices from the Global South aren’t afterthoughts but architects. Until then, institutions will keep being perceived as foreign entities imposing rules rather than partners building shared futures. And honestly, if we keep pretending neutrality when structures favor certain economies, we’re not solving the gap—we’re deepening it.
conversation.subtopic: Public perception gaps between nations regarding global institutions and their perceived legitimacy or effectiveness.

conversation.content: I’m skeptical that global institutions can ever truly bridge perception gaps when their decision-making remains concentrated in the same capitals—no amount of reform or rhetoric changes the fact that a farmer in Senegal doesn’t experience the IMF the same way a banker in Frankfurt does. These aren’t just cultural misunderstandings; they’re power imbalances dressed up as policy disagreements. And if legitimacy is supposed to come from inclusion, why do the loudest voices still come from those who designed the rules in the first place?
